rationale: Sort the arms by what they do to the protein, not by chemotype. The deletion removes PRMT7. The PROTAC also removes it: it recruits VHL and sends PRMT7 to the proteasome, mRNA untouched, and in T cells it lowers PRMT7 and raises nuclear p65 - the same molecular state as deletion - even though its warhead is the binder the inhibitor is built on. The catalytic inhibitor leaves the protein in place; because pre-treating with it abolishes degradation by the PROTAC, it demonstrably occupies PRMT7 in cells, so its arm tests loss of activity alone. Does losing activity equal losing the protein? No: the enzymatically dead mutant binds p65 and represses the reporter as well as wild type, so the brake on p65 is carried by the protein, not by methylation. Blocking the active site therefore leaves p65 restrained, whereas deletion or degradation releases it. Release sets the direction of the readout: PRMT7-deficient cells carry more nuclear p65, raised NF-kB targets including Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and CD25, and suppressed apoptosis programmes, and the CD8+ difference disappears under BAY 11-7082 - so both protein-removal arms push the CD8+ fraction up, not down. The arm in which CD8+ cells fell to about 11% against a ~30% control is therefore the catalytic inhibitor, SGC3027. Why blocking catalysis actively lowers the CD8+ fraction is not settled by these premises.
